title: Compute infra resilience checklist and recovery procedures (draft)
body:
TL;DR:
This is a pragmatic, lightweight runbook for common compute infra failures that touch GPU-backed nodes: partial GPU failures, degraded node behavior, safe cordon+drain for replacement, emergency capacity add, and short-cluster recovery steps. Use this when latency/p95 spikes, queued inference backlog increases for >5 minutes and the metrics point to diminished GPU capacity or node-level instability.

When to follow this runbook:
- Pager: SRE-Pager CPU/GPU (sev-2) triggered by enqueue/backlog or increased 5xxs tied to inference workers.
- Observability signs: sustained GPU utilization drop with running pods failing on CUDA initialisation, node kernel oops, repeated container restarts, or node NotReady for >60s.
- Business impact: host diagnostics indicate one or more GPU(s) unhealthy OR node-level kernel/OOM events.

Goals (order of priorities):
1) Contain and stop further degraded requests from hitting bad capacity.
2) Restore capacity quickly (either by replacing GPU, adding nodes, or routing to spare pools).
3) Preserve traces/eviction logs for post-incident RCA.
4) Return system to normal and create follow-up work.

Quick triage checklist (first 5 minutes):
- Identify affected node(s): check alert context, k8s events, and Aurora/cluster metrics.
  Commands: kubectl get nodes -o wide | egrep "NotReady|gpu"; kubectl describe node <node-name>
- Check node hardware health: ssh to node (jump via bastion), run nvidia-smi, dmesg | tail, journalctl -u kubelet --since "10m"
  Expected: nvidia-smi shows GPUs present and processes, or shows error codes.
- Identify affected pods: kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o 'wide' | grep <node-name>
- If node shows network flakiness or transient NotReady, consider cordon/drain to be safe.

Containment: cordon + safe drain
- Cordon node so scheduler doesn't place new pods: kubectl cordon <node-name>
- Evict safe workloads first (inference pods are preferred to move): kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --force --grace-period=30
  Notes: force only if pod does not respect grace. For critical stateful services, do manual move via scale down/up.
- If drain stalls due to local-path or long PVCs, annotate pod to allow eviction: kubectl patch pod <pod> -n <ns> -p '{"metadata":{"annotations":{"sre/evict-allowed":"true"}}}'
- If node is repeatedly flapping, temporarily scale down route weight (see Routing section) to keep traffic off the pool.

GPU replacement (hardware-level) - field tech + SRE collaboration
- Preconditions: node has a physical GPU fault (nvidia-smi shows xid errors, or dmesg has firmware/hw resets) and replacement SLA permits on-call swap. If unsure, escalate to Hardware Ops.
- Steps for field swap (summary for on-call):
  1) Put node into maintenance: kubectl cordon <node-name> (if not already).
  2) Ensure all inference pods are drained and running elsewhere. kubectl get pods -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node-name>
  3) Power off node per Data Center SOP (ticket to hardware ops): create hardware ticket with node serial, GPU model, and XID logs.
  4) Once GPU physically replaced, power on and monitor POST logs.
  5) On node boot, check kernel and nvidia modules: ssh -> sudo dmesg | grep -i nvidia; nvidia-smi; systemctl status nvidia-persistenced
  6) Rejoin node: kubectl uncordon <node-name> and verify pods can schedule.
- Quick verification: run a small canary inference job pinned to node (use debug pod with tolerations): kubectl run gpu-test --image=redwood/debug-gpu --overrides='{"apiVersion":"v1","spec":{"nodeName":"<node-name>"}}' --rm -it --restart=Never -- bash -c "python -c 'import torch; print(torch.cuda.is_available())'"

Node cordon/drain gotchas (lessons learned):
- DaemonSets may restart and show as running but can still fail GPU init — watch for GPU init logs inside the pod.
- Local data: some batch-preprocessor sidecars store checkpoints locally; confirm they are safe to delete or copy before forced drain.
- Evictions during heavy traffic: prefer rolling drains across nodes to avoid capacity cliff.

Emergency capacity add (fast path):
- If replacement will take >30-60m and backlog is growing, add capacity quickly:
  Cloud-managed cluster: scale nodepool via provider tooling (prefer same instance types and GPU count). Examples:
    - GCP: gcloud container node-pools update <pool> --cluster <cluster> --num-nodes <n>
    - EKS: eksctl scale nodegroup --cluster=<cluster> --name=<group> --nodes=<n>
body_continued:
- Self-hosted/terraform managed: comment in PR that triggers terraform apply for +N nodes (include instance type and region). If you are the on-call infra owner, run terraform apply after approval.
- If autoscaler exists, confirm cluster-autoscaler is healthy and not blocked by PodDisruptionBudgets. kubectl get deployment cluster-autoscaler -n kube-system
- After new nodes appear, verify they register with GPU drivers and the runtime. kubectl describe node <new-node> and nvidia-smi.

Routing and graceful degradation options:
- Routing layer (traffic proxy) can be used to move traffic off the degraded pool: update service weights in the routing config (Console -> Pools -> weigh down degraded pool). This is the fastest way to reduce user impact without touching nodes.
- Fallback to cheaper model variant: if latency and cost tradeoffs are OK, shift some traffic to a CPU-optimized model or smaller GPU model. This should be an automated policy for Dedicated customers; follow product SLOs.

Cluster recovery (control path degradation):
- If Kubernetes control plane shows API latency or unstable etcd leader changes, do not perform mass drains. Instead:
  1) Reduce change rate: stop CI/CD merges affecting infra, pause non-essential jobs.
  2) If ETCD is unhealthy, follow control-plane ETCD runbook (separate doc referenced).
  3) For transient API latency, add controller-manager replicas or scale API server if autoscaling available.

Post-incident checklist (immediately after service restored):
- Capture artifacts: kubectl get events --all-namespaces > /tmp/events-<incident>.log; collect node dmesg, nvidia-smi outputs, kubelet logs (journalctl -u kubelet).
- Create incident ticket summarizing actions, timeline, and metrics (attach artifacts).
- Run root-cause analysis within 3 business days; assign owners for hardware, infra, and product follow-ups.
- Update this runbook with any gaps discovered.

Observability and signals to record during incident:
- GPU error XID counts, driver version, kernel versions, pod restart counts, node NotReady durations, scheduler evictions, queue length and p95 latency for inference endpoints.
- Add temporary dashboard panels for the incident window and annotate them.

Short diagnostic commands cheat sheet (save locally):
- kubectl get nodes -o wide
- kubectl describe node <node>
- kubectl get pods --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node> -A
- ssh <node> sudo dmesg | tail -n 200
- ssh <node> nvidia-smi -q | head -n 80
- journalctl -u kubelet -n 200
- docker ps | grep gpu || crictl ps -a

Open questions / TODOs (for follow-up):
- Define exact XID thresholds that mandate immediate hardware replacement vs. reboot. (owner: Rafael)
- Add automated canary that runs lightweight inference on new/returned nodes and reports pass/fail to SRE channel. (owner: Jon)
- Document exact routing weight steps for Hosted vs Dedicated customers (owner: Product-Hosted-API).

Notes to self / on-call hints:
- In past incidents, a short kernel OOM during model load was masked by container restart loops — checking container logs is critical.
- When in doubt about hardware swap SLA, prioritize adding cloud capacity as a temporary mitigation.

References:
- Confluence: Compute Infra Home (see linked artifacts)
- Kubernetes drain/cordon docs and SRE incident postmortem template

Status: draft, needs signoff from Hardware Ops and Product-Hosted-API for routing changes.

End of document.
